report:
## Report

The evidence actually leans in the opposite direction from "no" — most current systematic reviews suggest honey **probably does help** relieve acute cough symptoms in children over age 1, though confidence in the size of the effect varies.

The most authoritative source, the **Cochrane systematic review** (Oduwole et al., updated 2018), found **moderate-certainty evidence** that honey reduces cough frequency and severity better than no treatment or placebo, and that cough resolved sooner with honey than with the asthma drug salbutamol. It also improved children's and parents' sleep quality (cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children; cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD007094.pub5/full).

A more recent 2023 systematic review published in the *European Journal of Pediatrics* reached a similar conclusion but rated the overall evidence quality as **low to very low**, due to small sample sizes, heterogeneity, and risk of bias in the underlying trials — meaning honey "may" help, but confirmation from larger, high-quality, blinded RCTs is still needed (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10570220/).

The **AAFP** and **Mayo Clinic** summaries align with this, stating honey can reduce cough frequency/severity and improve sleep compared with placebo or no treatment for children aged 1–18 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2016/0701/p20.html; mayoclinic.org/symptoms/cough/expert-answers/honey/faq-20058031).

**Important caveat:** honey must never be given to infants under 12 months due to risk of infant botulism from Clostridium botulinum spores (kidshealth.org/en/parents/honey-botulism.html).

**Conclusion:** The evidence does not support "no" — it supports a cautious "probably yes, for children over 1 year," with effect sizes modest and evidence certainty ranging from low to moderate depending on the review.
